# Preview

Ruff includes an opt-in preview mode to provide an opportunity for community feedback and increase confidence that
changes are a net-benefit before enabling them for everyone.

Preview mode enables a collection of unstable features such as new lint rules and fixes, formatter style changes, interface updates, and more. Warnings about deprecated features may turn into errors when using preview mode.

Enabling preview mode does not on its own enable all preview rules. See the [rules section](#using-rules-that-are-in-preview) for details on selecting preview rules.

## Enabling preview mode

Preview mode can be enabled with the `--preview` flag on the CLI or by setting `preview = true` in your Ruff
configuration file.

Preview mode can be configured separately for linting and formatting. To enable preview lint rules without preview style formatting:

=== "pyproject.toml"

    ```toml
    [tool.ruff.lint]
    preview = true
    ```

=== "ruff.toml"

    ```toml
    [lint]
    preview = true
    ```

=== "CLI"

    ```console
    ruff check --preview
    ```


To enable preview style formatting without enabling any preview lint rules:

=== "pyproject.toml"

    ```toml
    [tool.ruff.format]
    preview = true
    ```

=== "ruff.toml"

    ```toml
    [format]
    preview = true
    ```

=== "CLI"

    ```console
    ruff format --preview
    ```

## Using rules that are in preview

If a rule is marked as preview, it can only be selected if preview mode is enabled. For example, consider a
hypothetical rule, `HYP001`. If `HYP001` were in preview, it would _not_ be enabled by adding it to the selected rule set.

=== "pyproject.toml"

    ```toml
    [tool.ruff.lint]
    extend-select = ["HYP001"]
    ```

=== "ruff.toml"

    ```toml
    [lint]
    extend-select = ["HYP001"]
    ```

=== "CLI"

    ```console
    ruff check --extend-select HYP001
    ```


It also would _not_ be enabled by selecting the `HYP` category, like so:

=== "pyproject.toml"

    ```toml
    [tool.ruff.lint]
    extend-select = ["HYP"]
    ```

=== "ruff.toml"

    ```toml
    [lint]
    extend-select = ["HYP"]
    ```

=== "CLI"

    ```console
    ruff check --extend-select HYP
    ```


Similarly, it would _not_ be enabled via the `ALL` selector:

=== "pyproject.toml"

    ```toml
    [tool.ruff.lint]
    select = ["ALL"]
    ```

=== "ruff.toml"

    ```toml
    [lint]
    select = ["ALL"]
    ```

=== "CLI"

    ```console
    ruff check --select ALL
    ```

However, it _would_ be enabled in any of the above cases if you enabled preview mode:

=== "pyproject.toml"

    ```toml
    [tool.ruff.lint]
    extend-select = ["HYP"]
    preview = true
    ```

=== "ruff.toml"

    ```toml
    [lint]
    extend-select = ["HYP"]
    preview = true
    ```

=== "CLI"

    ```console
    ruff check --extend-select HYP --preview
    ```

To see which rules are currently in preview, visit the [rules reference](rules.md).

## Selecting single preview rules

When preview mode is enabled, selecting rule categories or prefixes will include all preview rules that match.
If you'd prefer to opt in to each preview rule individually, you can toggle the `explicit-preview-rules`
setting in your configuration file:

=== "pyproject.toml"

    ```toml
    [tool.ruff.lint]
    preview = true
    explicit-preview-rules = true
    ```

=== "ruff.toml"

    ```toml
    [lint]
    preview = true
    explicit-preview-rules = true
    ```

In our previous example, `--select` with `ALL` `HYP`, `HYP0`, or `HYP00` would not enable `HYP001`. Each preview
rule will need to be selected with its exact code: for example, `--select ALL,HYP001`.

If preview mode is not enabled, this setting has no effect.

## Deprecated rules

When preview mode is enabled, deprecated rules will be disabled. If a deprecated rule is selected explicitly, an
error will be raised. Deprecated rules will not be included if selected via a rule category or prefix.

# Proposing Lint Rules Rule suggestions can start out as brief issues. If a maintainer thinks the rule could be a good addition to Ruff, they will apply the `needs-design` label to suggest filling out the steps described below in support of the rule's acceptance. Some of this information will be easier to obtain with a working rule implementation and doesn't need to be present in the initial proposal. A design for a new lint rule in Ruff should include the following components: - A proposed name that follows our [rule naming convention](#rule-naming-convention) - A proposed category that follows our [rule categorization guidelines](#rule-categorization-guidelines) - A draft of the rule documentation with the following sections: - "What it does": a one line description of what the rule checks - "Why is this bad?": a longer explanation of the pattern flagged by the rule and why it causes problems in real projects - "Example": a code example showing the problematic code, as well as a code block showing the fixed code Some rules benefit from additional documentation. These sections usually emerge through the implementation process and aren't required in a design proposal. "Fix safety" and "Options" sections are required for rules with unsafe fixes and that rely on any settings, respectively, but the rest of these are fully optional. You can `grep` for each heading to see where they are often used. - "Known problems": any known limitations of the rule, such as false positives or negatives - "Fix availability": if the rule only has an autofix in some cases, explain why - "Fix safety": if the rule’s fix is ever unsafe, explain why - "Options": if the rule depends upon any configuration options, list them - "See also": if there are other similar or synergistic rules, list them - "References": if there are any relevant external references to Python or other documentation, list them A few examples of great rule documentation include [`mutable-argument-default` (`B006`)][b006], [`quoted-annotation` (`UP037`)][up037], and [`used-dummy-variable` (`RUF052`)][ruf052]. - An example diagnostic including the proposed name, primary message, and fix title (if applicable) This is another nice bonus that isn't required for a design proposal but concisely reveals a lot of helpful information about a rule. For example: ```markdown my-new-rule: primary diagnostic message --> example.py:1:1 1 | import math | ^^^^ help: fix title ``` When choosing a diagnostic range (marked by `^^^^` above), also consider that the start of the range determines where `noqa` comments will be valid ## Rule naming convention Like Clippy, Ruff's rule names should make grammatical and logical sense when read as "ignore ${rule}" or "ignore ${rule} items", as in the context of suppression comments. For example, `AssertFalse` fits this convention: it flags `assert False` statements, and so a suppression comment would be framed as "ignore `assert False`". As such, rule names should... - Highlight the pattern that is being linted against, rather than the preferred alternative. For example, `AssertFalse` guards against `assert False` statements. - _Not_ contain instructions on how to fix the violation, which instead belong in the rule documentation and the `fix_title`. - _Not_ contain a redundant prefix, like `Disallow` or `Banned`, which are already implied by the convention. When re-implementing rules from other linters, we prioritize adhering to this convention over preserving the original rule name. ## Rule categorization guidelines Choosing a category is a crucial part of the rule proposal and acceptance process. To paraphrase the [Clippy documentation](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2476-clippy-uno.html#what-lints-belong-in-clippy), if a rule doesn't fit in the categories, it probably doesn't fit in Ruff. Descriptions of each category can be found in the [rule category documentation](linter.md#rule-categories), but the flow chart below is intended to facilitate category assignment. ```mermaid --- config: flowchart: nodeSpacing: 20 rankSpacing: 25 padding: 8 themeVariables: fontSize: 13px --- flowchart TD A("Formatting, security,
or language restriction?") A -->|Yes| B["Formatting · Security · Restriction"] A -->|No| C("Too noisy or opinionated?") C -->|Yes| D["Pedantic"] C -->|No| E("Incorrect or deprecated?") E -->|Yes| F("Definitely wrong
today?") F -->|Yes| G["Correctness"] F -->|No| H["Suspicious"] E -->|No| I("Primary improvement?") I -->|Simpler| J["Complexity"] I -->|Faster| K["Performance"] I -->|Idiomatic| L["Style"] ``` The first question filters out special categories of rules: those that relate to the visual presentation of code (`formatting`), those that relate to `security` vulnerabilities, and those that impose `restriction`s on certain features. "Restriction" here specifically means an arbitrary or severe restriction, not the broad way in which any lint rule could be considered to restrict usage. Examples of restriction lints are rules like `assert` (`S101`) and `print` (`T201`), which ban basic language features across the board. If none of these special categories is quite right, the next question asks you to judge whether the rule is too noisy or opinionated for general use. This is somewhat subjective, but an [ecosystem report](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/contributing/#ecosystem-report) can be helpful to see how many diagnostics are emitted in real projects. A large number of diagnostics doesn't immediately make a rule `pedantic`, but many false positives or diagnostics that reasonable Python users would disagree with do. If a rule is not overly pedantic, we next consider the intention of the rule. If the main goal is detecting code that is incorrect, the options narrow to `correctness` or `suspicious`. Rules in the `correctness` category typically cause immediate issues like syntax or runtime errors, or silently do something the user didn't intend. Similarly, `suspicious` lints flag the same kind of code, but in cases where Ruff can't be sure what the user intended. A perfect example of a `suspicious` rule is `mutable-argument-default` (`B006`). This classic footgun is almost always a mistake, but in some cases, it may be intentional, in which case a `noqa` or `ruff: ignore` comment should be used. Such suppression comments should essentially never be reasonable for a `correctness` lint but are fine for `suspicious` lints. The `suspicious` category also includes deprecations, which aren't incorrect today but will cause errors in the future. The final branch of the flow chart deals with stylistic lints, which are again somewhat subjective to differentiate between changes that make code simpler often also make the code faster and more idiomatic. Thus, the question prompts you to consider the _primary_ improvement. Rules that primarily make code simpler are `complexity` lints, those that primarily make code faster or use less memory are `performance` lints, and those that primarily make code more idiomatic are `style`. ## Other guidelines Following these steps should generally ensure that a rule is a good fit for Ruff. A couple of additional things to watch out for are: - Rules that conflict with other tools, or especially other rules Although we have many existing `formatting` rules that overlap and even conflict with our formatter, we are not eager to add more. Similarly, we should avoid rules that mainly support type checker usage, when type checkers themselves emit similar diagnostics. Most clearly, we should avoid rules that overlap or conflict with other lint rules. This often suggests that the existing rule should instead be made configurable to toggle between the two behaviors. Checking both the input and output examples from your rule proposal with `ALL` rules selected in the [linter], with the [formatter], and with a [type checker] like ty is a good quick check for conflicts. - Rule

# Tutorial

This tutorial will walk you through the process of integrating Ruff's linter and formatter into
your project. For a more detailed overview, see [_Configuring Ruff_](configuration.md).

## Getting Started

To start, we'll initialize a project using [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/):

```console
$ uv init --lib numbers
```

This command creates a Python project with the following structure:

```text
numbers
  ├── README.md
  ├── pyproject.toml
  └── src
      └── numbers
          ├── __init__.py
          └── py.typed
```

We'll then clear out the auto-generated content in `src/numbers/__init__.py`
and create `src/numbers/calculate.py` with the following code:

```python
from typing import Iterable

import os


def sum_even_numbers(numbers: Iterable[int]) -> int:
    """Given an iterable of integers, return the sum of all even numbers in the iterable."""
    return sum(
        num for num in numbers
        if num % 2 == 0
    )
```

Next, we'll add Ruff to our project:

```console
$ uv add --dev ruff
```

We can then run the Ruff linter over our project via `uv run ruff check`:

```console
$ uv run ruff check
src/numbers/calculate.py:3:8: F401 [*] `os` imported but unused
Found 1 error.
[*] 1 fixable with the `--fix` option.
```

!!! note

    As an alternative to `uv run`, you can also run Ruff by activating the project's virtual
    environment (`source .venv/bin/activate` on Linux and macOS, or `.venv\Scripts\activate` on
    Windows) and running `ruff check` directly.

Ruff identified an unused import, which is a common error in Python code. Ruff considers this a
"fixable" error, so we can resolve the issue automatically by running `ruff check --fix`:

```console
$ uv run ruff check --fix
Found 1 error (1 fixed, 0 remaining).
```

Running `git diff` shows the following:

```diff
--- a/src/numbers/calculate.py
+++ b/src/numbers/calculate.py
@@ -1,7 +1,5 @@
 from typing import Iterable

-import os
-

def sum_even_numbers(numbers: Iterable[int]) -> int:
    """Given an iterable of integers, return the sum of all even numbers in the iterable."""
    return sum(
        num for num in numbers
        if num % 2 == 0
    )
```

Note Ruff runs in the current directory by default, but you can pass specific paths to check:

```console
$ uv run ruff check src/numbers/calculate.py
```

Now that our project is passing `ruff check`, we can run the Ruff formatter via `ruff format`:

```console
$ uv run ruff format
1 file reformatted
```

Running `git diff` shows that the `sum` call was reformatted to fit within the default 88-character
line length limit:

```diff
--- a/src/numbers/calculate.py
+++ b/src/numbers/calculate.py
@@ -3,7 +3,4 @@ from typing import Iterable

 def sum_even_numbers(numbers: Iterable[int]) -> int:
     """Given an iterable of integers, return the sum of all even numbers in the iterable."""
-    return sum(
-        num for num in numbers
-        if num % 2 == 0
-    )
+    return sum(num for num in numbers if num % 2 == 0)
```

Thus far, we've been using Ruff's default configuration. Let's take a look at how we can customize
Ruff's behavior.

## Configuration

To determine the appropriate settings for each Python file, Ruff looks for the first
`pyproject.toml`, `ruff.toml`, or `.ruff.toml` file in the file's directory or any parent directory.

To configure Ruff, we'll add the following to the configuration file in our project's root directory:

=== "pyproject.toml"

     ```toml
     [tool.ruff]
     # Set the maximum line length to 79.
     line-length = 79

     [tool.ruff.lint]
     # Add the `line-too-long` rule to the enforced rule set. By default, Ruff omits rules that
     # overlap with the use of a formatter, like Black, but we can override this behavior by
     # explicitly adding the rule.
     extend-select = ["E501"]
     ```

=== "ruff.toml"

     ```toml
     # Set the maximum line length to 79.
     line-length = 79

     [lint]
     # Add the `line-too-long` rule to the enforced rule set. By default, Ruff omits rules that
     # overlap with the use of a formatter, like Black, but we can override this behavior by
     # explicitly adding the rule.
     extend-select = ["E501"]
     ```

Running Ruff again, we see that it now enforces a maximum line width, with a limit of 79:

```console
$ uv run ruff check
src/numbers/calculate.py:5:80: E501 Line too long (90 > 79)
Found 1 error.
```

For a full enumeration of the supported settings, see [_Settings_](settings.md). For our project
specifically, we'll want to make note of the minimum supported Python version:

=== "pyproject.toml"

     ```toml
     [project]
     # Support Python 3.10+.
     requires-python = ">=3.10"

     [tool.ruff]
     # Set the maximum line length to 79.
     line-length = 79

     [tool.ruff.lint]
     # Add the `line-too-long` rule to the enforced rule set.
     extend-select = ["E501"]
     ```

=== "ruff.toml"

     ```toml
     # Support Python 3.10+.
     target-version = "py310"
     # Set the maximum line length to 79.
     line-length = 79

     [lint]
     # Add the `line-too-long` rule to the enforced rule set.
     extend-select = ["E501"]
     ```

### Rule Selection

Ruff supports [over 900 lint rules](rules.md) split across over 50 built-in plugins, but
determining the right set of rules will depend on your project's needs: some rules may be too
strict, some are framework-specific, and so on.

more, omitting any stylistic rules that overlap with the use of a formatter, like `ruff format` or
[Black](https://github.com/psf/black).

If you're introducing a linter for the first time, **the default rule set is a great place to
start**: it catches a wide variety of common errors (like unused imports) with zero configuration.
See [_Default Rules_](default-rules.md) for the complete list.

If you're migrating to Ruff from another linter, you can enable rules that are equivalent to
those enforced in your previous configuration. For example, if we want to enforce the pyupgrade
rules, we can set our configuration file to the following:

=== "pyproject.toml"

     ```toml
     [project]
     requires-python = ">=3.10"

     ]
     ```

     ```toml
     target-version = "py310"

     extend-select = [
       "UP",  # pyupgrade
     ]
     ```

all functions have docstrings:

     ```toml
     extend-select = [
       "UP",  # pyupgrade
       "D",   # pydocstyle
     ]
     ```

=== "ruff.toml"

Ruff uses a custom versioning scheme that uses the **minor** version number for breaking changes and the **patch** version number for bug fixes. Ruff does not yet have a stable API; once Ruff's API is stable, the **major** version number and semantic versioning will be used.

## Crate versioning

Ruff's crates are published to [crates.io](https://crates.io). The following crates follow Ruff's
normal versioning policy:

- `ruff`
- `ruff_linter`
- `ruff_wasm`

The Rust interfaces of these crates do not follow semantic versioning.

The remaining crates published as part of Ruff releases provide **no stability guarantees**. Their
Rust interfaces are considered internal and unstable. Consequently, they are versioned as `0.0.x`.
The patch version is incremented on every Ruff release, regardless of changes to the crate.

## Version changes

**Minor** version increases will occur when:

- A deprecated option or feature is removed
- Configuration changes in a backwards incompatible way
    - This _may_ occur in minor version changes until `1.0.0`, however, it should generally be avoided.
- Support for a new file type is promoted to stable
- Support for an end-of-life Python version is dropped
- Linter:
    - A rule is promoted to stable
    - The behavior of a stable rule is changed
        - The scope of a stable rule is significantly increased
        - The intent of the rule changes
        - Does not include bug fixes that follow the original intent of the rule
    - Stable rules are added to the default set
    - Stable rules are removed from the default set
    - A safe fix for a rule is promoted to stable
    - A rule is deprecated
- Formatter:
     - The stable style changed
- Language server:
    - An existing capability is removed
    - A deprecated server setting is removed

**Patch** version increases will occur when:

- Bugs are fixed, _including behavior changes that fix bugs_
- A new configuration option is added in a backwards compatible way (no formatting changes or new lint errors)
- Support for a new Python version is added
- Support for a new file type is added in preview
- An option or feature is deprecated
- Linter:
    - An unsafe fix for a rule is added
    - A safe fix for a rule is added in preview
    - The scope of a rule is increased in preview
    - A fix’s applicability is demoted
    - A rule is added in preview
    - The behavior of a preview rule is changed
- Formatter:
    - The stable style changed to prevent invalid syntax, changes to the program's semantics, or removal of comments
    - The preview style changed
- Language server:
    - Support for a new capability is added
    - A new server setting is added
    - A server setting is deprecated

## Minimum supported Rust version

The minimum supported Rust version required to compile Ruff is listed in the `rust-version` key of
the `[workspace.package]` section in `Cargo.toml`. It may change in any release (minor or patch). It
will never be newer than N-2 Rust versions, where N is the latest stable version. For example, if
the latest stable Rust version is 1.85, Ruff's minimum supported Rust version will be at most 1.83.

This is only relevant to users who build Ruff from source. Installing Ruff from the Python package
index usually installs a pre-built binary and does not require Rust compilation.

## Preview mode

A preview mode is available to enable new, unstable rules and features, e.g., support for a new file type.

The preview mode is intended to help us collect community feedback and gain confidence that changes are a net-benefit.

The preview mode is _not_ intended to gate access to work that is incomplete or features that we are _likely to remove._ However, **we reserve the right to make changes to _any_ behavior gated by the mode** including the removal of preview features or rules.

## Rule stabilization

When modifying or adding rules, we use the following guidelines:

- New rules should always be added in preview mode
- New rules will remain in preview mode for at least one minor release before being promoted to stable
    - If added in a patch release i.e. `0.6.1` then a rule will not be eligible for stability until `0.8.0`
- Stable rule behaviors are not changed significantly in patch versions
- Promotion of rules to stable may be delayed in order to “batch” them into a single minor release
- Not all rules in preview need to be promoted in a given minor release

## Fix stabilization

Fixes have three applicability levels:

- **Display**: Never applied, just displayed.
- **Unsafe**: Can be applied with explicit opt-in.
- **Safe**: Can be applied automatically.

Fixes for rules may be introduced at a lower applicability, then promoted to a higher applicability. Reducing the applicability of a fix is not a breaking change. The applicability of a given fix may change when the preview mode is enabled.

## Visual Studio Code Extension

Visual Studio Code [doesn't support pre-release
tags](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/working-with-extensions/publishing-extension#prerelease-extensions)
for extensions. Consequently, Ruff uses the following scheme to distinguish between stable and
preview releases:

Stable releases use even numbers in minor version component: `2024.30.0`, `2024.32.0`, `2024.34.0`, …
Preview releases use odd numbers in minor version component: `2024.31.0`, `2024.33.0`, `2024.35.0`, …

report.overview: Ruff 0.16.8 is Astral's Rust monorepo for a Python linter/formatter and the ty type checker. The user-facing `ruff` binary lints and formats Python (and notebooks) from the CLI, a stdio language server, or WASM; `ty` type-checks projects with a Salsa database and an optional uv integration. The PyPI package is a thin launcher around the native binary, not a Python implementation of the linter.

system_map.summary: The Cargo workspace (edition 2024, rust-version 1.96, toolchain channel 1.98.0) builds two binaries, `ruff` and `ty`, plus libraries they share: the Python parser and AST, diagnostics, and workspace settings. Ruff's check and format paths are parallel file walks over hierarchical TOML config with an on-disk `.ruff_cache`. ty is a separate CLI and language server on a Salsa 0.28 `ProjectDatabase`, with typeshed vendored under `crates/ty_vendored`. Release artifacts are a scratch Docker image, cargo-dist installers, PyPI (maturin bin binding), WASM playgrounds, and crate publishes, all driven from GitHub Actions.

claims.claim: The workspace members are `crates/*`, package version 0.16.8, Rust edition 2024, minimum rust-version 1.96, license MIT, and the shared dependency set includes both `ruff_*` crates and `ty_*` crates plus salsa 0.28.2.
The developer toolchain pin is Rust 1.98.0 in rust-toolchain.toml, which the Dockerfile copies before `rustup target add` and `cargo zigbuild --bin ruff --release`.

`ruff` starts at `crates/ruff/src/main.rs`: it expands `@file` args with `argfile`, parses `Args` with clap, and calls `ruff::run`. Windows uses mimalloc; other supported arches use jemalloc. Broken-pipe errors exit 0; other failures print `ruff failed` and return `ExitStatus::Error` (code 2).

`ty` starts at `crates/ty/src/main.rs` and calls `ty::run`. `ty::run` sets up Rayon, expands `@file` arguments, and dispatches `Cli` to check, server, version, shell completion, or explain. Exit statuses are Success 0, Failure 1, Error 2, InternalError 101, and Interrupted 130.

PyPI packaging uses maturin with `bindings = "bin"`, `manifest-path = "crates/ruff/Cargo.toml"`, and `python-source = "python"`. `python/ruff/__main__.py` execs (or on Windows `subprocess.run`s) the native binary located by `find_ruff_bin`, which searches sysconfig script directories rather than embedding the linter in Python.

Shared front-end: `ruff_python_parser::parse` builds a `Parsed<Mod>` via `Parser::new`, and both the linter (`lint_only`) and the formatter (`format_module_source`) consume that parse. The linter crate documents its public API as completely unstable.

Ruff settings come from `ruff_workspace`. `project_files_in_path` normalizes paths, walks ancestors for `pyproject.toml` when hierarchical discovery is on, and walks the tree with the `ignore` crate's `WalkBuilder` (gitignore on, hidden files included, at most 12 threads).

Lint/format caches live in `.ruff_cache` (`ruff_cache::CACHE_DIR_NAME`). `Cache::open` stores one rkyv file per package at `cache_dir/VERSION/<settings key>` and drops entries if the package root does not match.

ty's persistent state is a Salsa `ProjectDatabase` created by `ProjectDatabase::fallible`. `check` and `check_with_reporter` delegate to `Project::check`. One-shot CLI checks call `disable_lru` and may `freeze` inputs; `run_check` then `mem::forget`s the database after optional `TY_MEMORY_REPORT` dumps.

Language servers are separate crates speaking stdio LSP: `ruff server` calls `ruff_server::run` (worker threads capped at 4); `ty server` calls `ty_server::run_server` with an `OsSystem` fallback and the same thread cap.

Release shape is cargo-dist 0.31.0 (`dist = false` on the workspace, local artifact jobs `./build-binaries`, `./build-docker`, `./build-wasm`; publish jobs PyPI, wasm, and crates). Installers are shell and PowerShell for a long target list, hosted at `https://releases.astral.sh/github/ruff/releases/download/{tag}`. The Docker image is `FROM scratch` with `ENTRYPOINT ["/ruff"]` and `WORKDIR /io`.

In-browser entry points are `ruff_wasm` (`Workspace::new` deserializes `Options` into `Settings`) and the npm workspaces `ruff`, `ty`, and `shared` under `playground/`, built with Vite, React, Tailwind, and wasm-pack. Sharing uses a Cloudflare Worker in `playground/api`.

feature_catalog.summary: Ruff's clap `Command` enum is the product surface: lint, format, an LSP server, rule and config help, cache cleaning, shell completions, and an import graph. The linter reimplements a large set of Flake8-family plugins as native rules under `ruff_linter::rules`, selected by code or category. ty exposes check (with fix and ignore insertion), a language server, and `explain rule`. Both tools have WASM playgrounds; Ruff also formats notebooks and can watch the filesystem.

claims.claim: `ruff check` (`CheckCommand`) accepts paths or `-` for stdin, `--fix` / `--fix-only` / `--diff` / `--unsafe-fixes`, `--watch`, `--ignore-noqa`, `--add-noqa` and `--add-ignore`, `--select` / rule selectors, `--target-version`, `--preview`, and `--output-format` from `RUFF_OUTPUT_FORMAT` plus `--output-file` from `RUFF_OUTPUT_FILE`. `--show-settings` and `--show-files` short-circuit before linting.

Default fix behavior generates fixes but does not write them. `--diff` selects `FixMode::Diff`; `--fix` or `--fix-only` selects `FixMode::Apply`; otherwise `FixMode::Generate`. Applicability stays automatic unless `--unsafe-fixes` is set. `--add-noqa` / `--add-ignore` refuse newlines in the reason and are incompatible with `--fix`.

`ruff format` (`FormatCommand`) writes files by default. `--diff` selects `FormatMode::Diff` and `--check` selects `FormatMode::Check`. `--range` is rejected when the resolved path set contains more than one file. Stdin is handled by `commands::format_stdin::format_stdin` instead of `commands::format::format`.

Formatting itself is `format_module_source`: parse with `ParseOptions` from the source type, build `TriviaRanges`, `format_module_ast`, then `print`. Parse, format, and print failures become `FormatModuleError` and map to `DiagnosticId::InternalError`.

`ruff server` is the editor integration. Request handlers registered in `ruff_server` are code action, code-action resolve, document diagnostic, execute command, format, format range, hover, and shutdown. Notifications include didOpen/didChange/didClose for text documents and notebooks, configuration, watched files, and workspace changes. Code-action kinds include `source.fixAll.ruff` and `source.organizeImports.ruff` (plus notebook variants).

Other Ruff subcommands: `rule` (one rule or `--all`), `config` (one option or the catalog), `linter` (upstream linter list), `clean`, hidden `generate-shell-completion`, `version`, and `analyze graph` (`AnalyzeGraphCommand`: direction, string-import detection, `--python` venv, type-checking imports, preview, target version).

Native lint plugins are the `Linter` enum in `registry.rs` (prefixes such as AIR, E/W via pycodestyle, F, S, B, I, UP, PL, RUF) and matching modules under `crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/` (`airflow` through `tryceratops`, including `pyflakes`, `pylint`, `pyupgrade`, `isort`, `flake8_bugbear`, `ruff`). `code_to_rule` is the `#[ruff_macros::map_codes]` table that maps `(Linter, code)` to a rule struct.

`ty` subcommands are `check`, `server`, `version`, hidden `generate-shell-completion`, and `explain rule`. `ty check` takes paths, `--project`, `--config-file`, `--fix`, `--add-ignore`, `--watch`, `--exit-zero`, color, verbosity, and progress flags. Fix mode is `FixMode::ApplyFixes` or `FixMode::AddIgnore`; plain runs are `MainLoopMode::Check`.

ty diagnostics come from `ty_python_semantic::check_file`: I/O errors, parse errors, unsupported-syntax errors (with an inferred-version hint), then `check_types`. Lints are `LintMetadata` values created with `declare_lint!` (kebab-case name, summary, docs, default `Level` of ignore/warn/error, status) and stored in `default_lint_registry`.

The Ruff WASM API exposes `Workspace` with `version`, a constructor from JS `Options`, and `defaultSettings`. The playground README describes two SPAs (Ruff at play.ruff.rs and a ty playground) using Monaco, Vite, and localStorage, plus a Worker KV share store.

Notebooks are first-class inputs: watch mode treats `.py`, `.pyi`, `.pyw`, and `.ipynb` as source and `.toml` as configuration, and `lint_path` lints `pyproject.toml` / `ruff.toml` when a TOML rule is enabled via `lint_fix_toml` / `lint_toml`.

`cargo dev` (`crates/ruff_dev`) is the maintainer CLI: `generate-all`, JSON schemas, rules tables, options docs, ty CLI/env/schema docs, `print-ast` / `print-cst` / `print-tokens`, formatter stability (`format-dev`), and `repeat` for profiling `ruff check`.

data_flow.summary: Ruff and ty both start from OS arguments and project files, never from a network service in the CLI. Ruff turns paths into per-file source text, a parse, noqa/suppression directives, and diagnostics, then either prints them, writes fixes, or stores a negative cache entry. ty loads project metadata into a Salsa database, type-checks files in parallel, and optionally rewrites source. The only intentional subprocess is uv, and only when `TY_UV` enables it. The playground is the network boundary: the browser runs WASM locally and optionally POSTs source to Workers KV.

claims.claim: Input boundary for both CLIs is `wild::args_os` expanded by `argfile::expand_args_from` (prefix `@`) before clap parsing. Ruff also honors `FORCE_COLOR` via `colored_override` and `RUFF_OUTPUT_FORMAT` / `RUFF_OUTPUT_FILE`.

`ruff check` calls `resolve::resolve` for the root config, then `project_files_in_path`. Enabled rules decide whether `.py` and pyproject/ruff TOML files stay in the set. Package roots come from `resolver.package_roots`, and per-file `LinterSettings` come from `resolver.resolve(path)`.

Per-file lint transform in `diagnostics::lint_path`: cache lookup by relative path plus `FileCacheKey` (mtime and permission mode); on miss, `SourceKind::from_path`; then `lint_fix` (apply or diff) or `lint_only`. `lint_only` parses, builds `Locator`, `Stylist`, and `Indexer`, extracts noqa directives and `Suppressions`, and calls `check_path`.

`check_path` is phased: token rules, filesystem rules, logical-line rules, then (only if the parse is valid) `check_ast` plus import sorting and docstring line collection, then physical-line rules. AST checking is `checkers::ast::check_ast`. Diagnostics are sorted with `Diagnostic::ruff_start_ordering` before return.

Output boundary for a check: `Printer` writes violations to stdout, or to `RUFF_OUTPUT_FILE` (parent directories created, color forced off) unless `--watch`. `--fix` writes transformed source with `File::create`; `--diff` writes a unified diff to stdout. Watch mode uses `notify::recommended_watcher` and re-resolves config when a `.toml` changes.

Cache write path: after the parallel fold, `caches.persist()` runs `Cache::persist`, which rkyv-serializes `PackageCache` to a temp file in the cache directory and renames it into place. Windows `PermissionDenied` on that rename is warned, not failed. A cache hit with noqa enabled returns empty diagnostics and skips re-lint.

ty input flow: cwd from `current_directory`, optional `--project` directory, absolute check paths, `OsSystem`, and `UseUv::from_system`. Metadata is `ProjectMetadata::from_config_file` or `discover_with_uv`, then `apply_configuration_files` and `set_override_options`. A single PEP 723 script file forces `UseUv::Scripts` even when uv is otherwise on.

ty check execution: `MainLoop::main_loop` synchronizes script environments, then on `CheckWorkspace` clones the database and Rayon-spawns `db.check_with_reporter`. `Project::check` reports settings and file-set diagnostics, then `into_par_iter` calls salsa `check_file_impl`, which calls `ty_python_semantic::check_file` unless script settings are invalid. Results are discarded if the revision moved.

ty fix output: `FixMode::ApplyFixes` calls `fix_all_diagnostics` with `Applicability::Safe` only; `FixMode::AddIgnore` calls `suppress_all_diagnostics`. `--exit-zero` forces `ExitStatus::Success` after a non-internal result. `TY_MEMORY_REPORT=short|full|json` dumps Salsa memory on the summary stream.

When uv is enabled, `Uv::execute` runs `Command::new(executable)` with args `workspace metadata --quiet`. Workspace targets add `--active`; script targets add `--sync --script <path>` and optional `--python`. The executable is `UV` if set, otherwise `system.which("uv")`.

Playground data flow: the SPA keeps editor state in localStorage and runs Ruff or ty as WASM. Share URLs hit the Worker: GET `/{id}` reads Workers KV namespace `PLAYGROUND`; POST reads the raw body, stores it under `crypto.randomUUID()`, and returns the id. Production CORS allows `https://play.ruff.rs` plus `playknot.ruff.rs`, `types.ruff.rs`, and `play.ty.dev`.

behavior_traces.summary: Three user-visible pipelines dominate: process startup for each binary, `ruff check` from arguments to printed diagnostics and cache, and `ty check` from project discovery through a cancellable Salsa main loop. Format and the Ruff language server are the same file pipeline entered from different adapters. Watch modes re-enter those pipelines on filesystem events instead of exiting.

claims.claim: Ruff startup order: `main` enables Windows virtual terminal, expands args, `Args::parse_from`, `run`. `run` applies color, `ruff_db::set_program_version`, installs a panic hook that points at the GitHub issue URL, skips logging for `Command::Server`, then matches `Command` to `check`, `format`, `server`, `analyze_graph`, or the help commands.

`ruff check` order: `CheckCommand::partition` -> `resolve::resolve` -> optional `show_settings` / `show_files` -> compute `FixMode` -> if suppression flags, `commands::add_noqa::add_noqa` and return -> else build `Printer` -> if `--watch`, `recommended_watcher` and an initial `commands::check::check` -> otherwise the same `check` once.

`commands::check::check` order: `project_files_in_path` -> retain Python and ruff/pyproject TOML -> `package_roots` -> `PackageCacheMap::init` if cache enabled -> `paths.par_iter` calling `lint_path` -> `catch_unwind` around `diagnostics::lint_path` -> fold/reduce diagnostics -> `sort_by(Diagnostic::ruff_start_ordering)` -> `caches.persist`. A panic becomes `create_panic_diagnostic` instead of aborting the process.

`diagnostics::lint_path` order for Python: `FileCacheKey::from_path` and `cache.get` -> `settings.extension.get_source_type` -> `SourceKind::from_path` -> `lint_fix` or `lint_only` -> on `FixMode::Apply`, `transformed.write` to `File::create(path)`; on `Diff`, write `source_kind.diff` to stdout. TOML files branch earlier into `lint_fix_toml` / `lint_toml`.

`lint_only` order: `settings.resolve_target_version` -> `ParseSource::into_parsed` -> `Locator::new` -> `Stylist::from_tokens` -> `Indexer::from_tokens` -> `directives::extract_directives` -> `Suppressions::from_tokens` -> `check_path`. `lint_fix` repeats that loop up to 100 iterations, tracking `FixTable`.

`ruff format` order: `FormatCommand::partition` -> `resolve::resolve` -> `resolve_default_files` -> `project_files_in_path` -> `package_roots` -> optional `PackageCacheMap::init` -> parallel per-path format. Each file reaches `format_module_source` -> `parse` -> `format_module_ast` -> `Printed`.

ty startup and check order: `main` -> `run` -> `setup_rayon` -> `Cli::parse_from` -> `run_check` -> `setup_tracing` -> resolve cwd/project/paths -> `UseUv::from_system` -> `ProjectMetadata::{from_config_file|discover_with_uv}` -> `ProjectDatabase::fallible` -> `MainLoop::new` -> `ctrlc::set_handler` -> `watch` or `run`.

ty main-loop order: `synchronize_scripts` -> `request_check` -> biased select on uv sync wakeups, watcher messages, and check requests. `CheckWorkspace` defers while `has_pending_synchronizations`, else spawns `check_with_reporter` + `into_sorted_diagnostics`. `CheckCompleted` either `write_diagnostics` or `fix_all_diagnostics` / `suppress_all_diagnostics`. Ctrl+C calls `CancellationTokenSource::stop`.

Per-file ty order inside `check_file_impl`: if the file is a script without valid settings, return script settings diagnostics; else `ty_python_semantic::check_file`; then append script settings diagnostics and a dependency-metadata diagnostic. `check_file` itself loads `source_text`, returns `IOErrorDiagnostic` on read error, extends parse and unsupported-syntax diagnostics, extends `check_types`, and sorts by `rendering_sort_key`.

Ruff LSP diagnostic order: `publish_diagnostics_for_document` calls `generate_diagnostics`, which no-ops unless `client_settings().lint()`, otherwise `crate::lint::check` on the document snapshot, then `Client::send_notification` of `PublishDiagnosticsNotification` per URI with the document version. Server boot is `ConnectionInitializer::stdio` then `Server::new(...).run` and `io_threads.join`.

Cache persistence order on a dirty cache: `Cache::persist` -> `save` merges changes -> `tempfile_in(parent)` -> `rkyv::to_bytes` of `PackageCache` -> `write_all` -> `NamedTempFile::persist`. No-change caches return before opening a temp file.

testing_signals.summary: Tests are Rust-native: cargo-nextest in CI, insta snapshots, and ty Markdown fixtures executed by `datatest-stable`. Parser, linter, and formatter crates carry large snapshot and fixture trees; the Ruff CLI has integration tests under `crates/ruff/tests`. CI path-filters which jobs run, and additionally dogfoods `ty check` on in-repo Python. Fuzz targets cover parse, fix, and format idempotency. Playground Worker code and file-watching tests are the obvious gaps.

claims.claim: Linux CI job `cargo test (linux)` runs `uv run --locked --only-dev cargo insta test --all-features --unreferenced reject --test-runner nextest --disable-nextest-doctest`, then `cargo test --doc --all-features`. It is skipped when the PR has label `no-test` or `determine_changes` says no code changed (except on main).

The same job dogfoods ty: `cargo run -p ty check` on `python/py-fuzzer`, `scripts/ty_benchmark`, and `scripts/*.py` (the last with `TY_UV=scripts` and `UV_LOCKED=true`). A prior step runs `cargo test -p ty_python_semantic --test mdtest` with `MDTEST_GITHUB_ANNOTATIONS_FORMAT=1` and ignores its exit code so annotations cannot fail the job.

CI also runs `cargo fmt`, `shellcheck`, `cargo clippy` (including a wasm clippy job), `cargo hawk` at HAWK_VERSION 0.1.13, and a `cargo publish` dry-run. `determine_changes` sets outputs `parser`, `linter`, `formatter`, `ty`, `playground`, `fuzz`, `py-fuzzer`, `benchmarks`, and `release` from path filters. Workflow permissions are `contents: read`.

ty semantic tests are Markdown files. `crates/ty_python_semantic/tests/mdtest.rs` registers `mdtest` and `lint_doc` via datatest-stable; each fixture runs on a one-thread Rayon pool. `lint_doc` looks the filename stem up in `default_lint_registry` and passes it as `default_error_rule`. Fixtures live under `./resources/mdtest` and `./resources/lint_docs`.

Ruff CLI coverage includes `crates/ruff/tests` (integration and CLI snapshot tests) and a unit test `unreadable_files` in `commands/check.rs` that creates mode-0o000 files and snapshots E902 / invalid-pyproject diagnostics with insta. Rule crates keep insta snapshots beside rules (for example `rules/pyflakes` and `rules/pylint`).

Parser tests are fixture-driven: `crates/ruff_python_parser/resources` holds hundreds of `.py` fixtures and `crates/ruff_python_parser/tests` holds matching snapshots. Formatter tests similarly pair `resources/test` fixtures with `tests` snapshots. The parser fuzz target `ruff_parse_simple` and idempotency target `ruff_parse_idempotency` sit outside the workspace.

Fuzz package `ruff-fuzz` (separate `[workspace]`, cargo-fuzz, libfuzzer-sys) builds bins `ty_check_invalid_syntax`, `ruff_parse_simple`, `ruff_fix_validity`, `ruff_formatter_validity`, `ruff_parse_idempotency`, and `ruff_formatter_idempotency`. It depends on the linter, parser, formatter, and ty semantic crates with the semantic `testing` feature.

AGENTS.md requires `INSTA_FORCE_PASS=1 INSTA_UPDATE=always MDTEST_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 cargo nextest run` (or `cargo test` if nextest is missing), forbids hand-editing snapshot bodies, and says file-watcher tests do not work in the sandbox. Clippy gate is `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`.

`pyproject.toml` defines a `ruff-lsp-test` dependency group (pytest, pygls 1.x, lsprotocol) separate from the Rust LSP crates, and a `ty-ecosystem` group on `ecosystem-analyzer`. Those are integration/ecosystem harnesses, not the in-crate nextest suites.

The playground Worker (`playground/api/src/index.ts`) has no test module beside it, and `playground/package.json` scripts are `dev:wasm`, oxlint, `tsc`, and prettier rather than a behavioral test runner. WASM API tests exist as `crates/ruff_wasm/tests/api.rs` and `crates/ty_wasm/tests/api.rs`, which is a different layer.
An ignored `linter_quick_test` in `ruff_linter` is an ad-hoc debug entry point (`#[ignore]`) that runs one rule through `test_contents`. It is not part of normal CI coverage.

risk_map.summary: The repository's own threat model treats project source and config as attacker-controlled and forbids analysis from executing that code. The sharp edges that do cross a process or network boundary are ty's uv subprocess, fix/format writes, cache files, stdio LSP, and the unauthenticated playground share API. Internally, the rule table in `codes.rs`, Salsa cancellation, and the unstable linter API are the maintenance blast radii.

claims.claim: The CLI threat model states analysis must not execute user-supplied code; `--isolated` must ignore config files; reading files reached via imports, config extensions, or symlinks is expected; fixes, format, ignore insertion, and cache cleanup may change only the operation's selected targets; `ruff format --check` must not write source.

ty's uv integration is off unless `TY_UV` is `1`, `true` (`UseUv::On`), or `scripts` (`UseUv::Scripts`). When on, `Uv::execute` runs the `UV` env var or `PATH`'s `uv`. Script metadata uses `workspace metadata --sync --script`, which the threat model says may install dependencies.

`--fix` and format `Write` mode replace file contents via `File::create` and a full write of the transformed source. A failed fix falls back to `lint_only` on the original. `--add-noqa` also rewrites files. These are the intentional mutation paths.

Cache files are written outside the source tree only in the sense that `.ruff_cache` (or `cache-dir`) sits in the project and is excluded from linting by default. Persistence is atomic rename, but a mismatched package root silently clears `package.files`, and unreadable cache files are replaced with an empty cache after a warning.

The playground share Worker stores the entire POST body in KV with a random UUID and no authentication, size check, or content-type check in `fetch`. GET returns the stored text to any caller who has the id. Production CORS is an allowlist, not an auth scheme. Dev mode sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.

Both language servers read editor documents over stdio and trust the client connection. Ruff publishes diagnostics from in-memory snapshots (`snapshot.query()`), so a hostile document is linted with the server's filesystem rights. ty's server additionally requires a Unicode cwd and keeps an `OsSystem` fallback for files not in the index.

Python launcher risk is local binary lookup: `find_ruff_bin` returns the first `ruff` executable on a fixed list of script directories and `__main__` `execvp`s it. A planted binary earlier in that search list would run with the user's privileges. On Windows the launcher uses `subprocess.run` and maps `KeyboardInterrupt` to exit 2.

Lint panics are isolated per file with `catch_unwind` and reported as diagnostics, but `Cache::open` and the Windows color setup still use `unwrap`/`assert` on paths that are not panic-isolated (`SystemTime::UNIX_EPOCH.elapsed().unwrap()`, `set_virtual_terminal` assert). ty's check thread uses `salsa::Cancelled::catch` and drops stale revisions.

`codes.rs` `code_to_rule` is a single macro-expanded match from every rule code to a rule type. A new rule that is not added there is unreachable from `--select` and noqa codes. `Rule::from_code` searches `Linter::all_rules` by noqa suffix.

ty one-shot checks `freeze` the database and then `std::mem::forget(db)` so destructors do not run. `system_mut` documents that it cancels other handles and can deadlock if the refcount is not 1. Watch mode, fix modes, and memory reports must not freeze.

The linter library is explicitly unstable. WASM, the CLI, and the language server all call into `check_path` / settings types, so a signature change in `ruff_linter` fans out across `crates/ruff`, `ruff_server`, and `ruff_wasm`.

Docker build fetches rustup with `curl | sh` and compiles a musl binary. That is a release-supply-chain path, not a runtime path for users of the scratch image. cargo-dist comments that CI customizes cargo-dist install specifically to avoid `curl | sh` for the dist tool itself.

Debug Ruff builds warn when the cache is left on, because `--no-cache` is what developers expect while iterating. Shipping a debug binary to users would both warn and serve potentially stale-looking cache behavior relative to source edits.

extension_points.summary: New Ruff rules plug into a plugin module, the `Linter` enum, and the `code_to_rule` table, usually scaffolded by `scripts/add_rule.py`. New ty lints plug into `declare_lint!` plus `LintRegistryBuilder::register_lint`. User-facing commands, LSP methods, TOML options, and WASM settings are each a closed table that must be updated and then regenerated into docs and JSON schema. Checker phases and `FormatNodeRule` are the extension points inside an existing rule or syntax node.

claims.claim: `scripts/add_rule.py` scaffolds a rule (`--name`, `--prefix`, `--code`, `--linter`, `--category`). The implementation then lives under `crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/<plugin>/` and must be referenced from `code_to_rule` in `codes.rs`. Plugin modules are declared in `rules/mod.rs`.

`Linter` is a `RuleNamespace` enum. `#[derive(RuleNamespace)]` in `ruff_macros` generates the prefix and rule-iteration impls. `Rule::from_code` parses a code into that namespace and matches the noqa suffix.

Rule structs use `#[derive(ViolationMetadata)]` (`ruff_macros::derive_violation_metadata`). `Violation` and `AlwaysFixableViolation` are the public traits re-exported from `ruff_linter`. Test-only rules are compiled in under `feature = "test-rules"` inside `check_path`.

ty lints are not in the Ruff `Rule` enum. `declare_lint!` builds a `LintMetadata` static; `register_lints` in `ty_python_semantic` calls `types::register_lints` and then registers ignore-comment lints. `LintRegistryBuilder::register_lint` panics on a duplicate name. Aliases go through `register_alias`.

CLI extension is the clap `Command` enum in `crates/ruff/src/args.rs` and the match in `ruff::run`. ty's parallel table is `crates/ty/src/args.rs` `Command` and the match in `ty::run`. Hidden shell-completion variants call `clap_complete_command`.

Ruff LSP methods are one module per request under `server/api/requests/` and one per notification under `server/api/notifications/`, re-exported from `requests.rs` and `notifications.rs`. Adding a method means a new handler type plus registration in those modules, not a dynamic plugin loader.

Configuration options use `#[derive(OptionsMetadata)]` and `CombineOptions` from `ruff_macros`. `ruff config` prints that metadata. `cargo dev generate-all` / `generate-json-schema` / `generate-options` / `generate-ty-schema` regenerate `ruff.schema.json`, `ty.schema.json`, and docs. CLI overrides arrive as `ConfigurationTransformer` implementations passed into `resolve_root_settings`.

Lint passes are selected by `rule.lint_source()` inside `check_path`: tokens, filesystem, logical lines, AST, imports, physical lines, and TOML. A rule that needs a new pass has to extend that match of sources, not only the rule body. AST work enters through `check_ast`.

Formatter node coverage is the `FormatNodeRule<N>` trait (`fmt` handles comments and source-map positions; `fmt_fields` is implemented per node). `format_module_ast` is the stable entry for callers that already have a `Parsed<Mod>`.

WASM settings are whatever `Options` / `Configuration::from_options` accepts. `Workspace::new` is the JS constructor; `defaultSettings` re-serializes defaults including `DEFAULT_SELECTORS`. There is no runtime plugin registry in the WASM crate.

File discovery can be customized per invocation by implementing `ConfigurationTransformer` and passing it to `project_files_in_path` / `resolve_scoped_settings`. The CLI's `ConfigArguments` is that transformer for `--config` key/value overrides and `--isolated`.

agent_handoff.summary: Read the CLI dispatch and the crate you are changing before editing; Ruff and ty share a parser but not a rule registry. Semantic changes need a focused test, snapshot updates via the environment variables rather than hand edits, and `cargo dev generate-all` when options, rules, or CLI help change. ty code must keep `db` in the Salsa parameter position and must not touch another file's AST from an untracked query. Do not drop Python repros inside this checkout, and do not expect file-watcher tests to pass in a sandbox.

claims.claim: Start with `AGENTS.md` (test commands, mdtest style, Salsa rules, `db` parameter order, prek) and `crates/ruff/src/lib.rs` plus `args.rs` for Ruff CLI work, or `crates/ty/src/lib.rs` for ty CLI work. Rule work starts at `codes.rs` `code_to_rule` and the plugin module; ty lint work starts at `declare_lint!` and `register_lints`.

Safe Ruff lint edit: add or change a rule under `crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/<plugin>/`, register it in `code_to_rule`, add a fixture and insta snapshot, and leave unrelated plugins alone. The public `ruff_linter` API is documented as unstable, so do not churn signatures to make a single rule compile.

Tests to run for a linter change: `cargo nextest run -p ruff_linter` (or the narrower test binary) with `INSTA_FORCE_PASS=1 INSTA_UPDATE=always MDTEST_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1`, then review snapshot diffs. For ty semantic changes, run `cargo nextest run -p ty_python_semantic --test mdtest`. Full CI uses `cargo insta test --all-features --unreferenced reject --test-runner nextest`.

Never edit `.snap` files or inline snapshot bodies by hand. After option, CLI, rule, or environment-variable definition changes, run `cargo dev generate-all` so `ruff.schema.json`, `ty.schema.json`, and generated docs stay aligned. Finish with `uv run --only-dev --locked prek run --files <each changed path>`.

ty parameter convention: `db` is the first argument of free functions and comes immediately after `self` on methods. Methods that read `.node()` should be `#[salsa::tracked]`. `check_file_impl` is already a tracked query; do not call raw AST helpers from module A while checking module B.

Ad-hoc Python repros must be created outside the checkout. The root `pyproject.toml` sets `requires-python = ">=3.7"` and `tool.ruff.target-version = "py38"`, so ty discovered from this tree infers an old Python version. ty preview for 3.15 is still warned unless preview is enabled.

Do not use `panic!`, `unreachable!`, `unwrap`, or `expect` for conditions the type system can encode. Existing exceptions include the Windows VT assert in `main` and cache timestamp truncation; do not add more. Lint-path failures should become diagnostics the way `catch_unwind` already does.
ty PR titles should start with `[ty]`. LSP-only changes use the `server` label when you can set labels. Avoid competing with an open PR; `CONTRIBUTING.md` is the duplicate-work check.

File-watcher tests do not work in the sandbox. Ruff watch mode is `recommended_watcher` in `ruff::check`; ty watch mode is `watch::directory_watcher` plus `ProjectWatcher`. Skip those locally unless the change is specifically about watching.

Cache keys include the crate version string, so behavior changes that should invalidate user caches need a version bump or an explicit settings-key change. Do not hand-delete logic that compares `package.package_root` or the atomic rename; both exist because of real corruption bugs.

Formatter and parser changes have their own fixture trees and fuzz targets (`ruff_formatter_idempotency`, `ruff_parse_idempotency`). A parser change that still snap-passes can fail idempotency fuzz; run the crate tests, not only a single rule snapshot.

Security-sensitive edits (subprocess, LSP trust, playground KV, cache paths, fix application) should be checked against `agents/references/cli-threat-model.md`, `language-server-threat-model.md`, `playground-threat-model.md`, or `repository-threat-model.md` as appropriate. uv must stay default-off.
